1.title: Undoing and Recovering
1.text: Welcome to Module six: Undoing and Recovering. It covers the exam area Part two: Branching and history. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. Discard or unstage changes with restore. Clean untracked files safely. Undo local commits with amend and reset. Undo shared commits with revert, including a merge. Park work with stash. Copy a commit with cherry-pick. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Course
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the course. Part: Part two: Branching and history. Verified with: Git two point five zero.one: every command was run in the lab.

1.title: Undo changes you have not committed
1.text: Undo changes you have not committed. Every undo starts with one question: where is the change right now? Git keeps it in the working tree, in the staging area, in a local commit, or on the remote. Each place has its own undo command, as the figure shows.

1.title: Undo changes you have not committed, continued
1.text: Undo changes you have not committed. The figure shows this: The undo commands placed on the Git areas: restore works on the working tree and the staging area, reset moves the branch, revert adds a commit on top, and the reflog finds lost commits.

1.title: Undo changes you have not committed, continued
1.text: Undo changes you have not committed. git restore file. Discards the edit in the working tree. Git never saved it, so there is no undo. git restore the staged flag file. Unstages the file; the edit stays in the working tree. git restore the source flag set to head tilde one file. Brings back the file as it was in an older commit, as an unstaged change. git clean dash n, then git clean dash f. Previews, then deletes untracked files.

1.title: Undo changes you have not committed, continued
1.text: Undo changes you have not committed. git restore does not know untracked files, so git restore scratch dot txt fails. Older guides use git checkout -- file, which still works. git clean refuses to run without dash f. By default it keeps untracked directories ( dash d includes them) and ignored files ( dash x includes them). Try it. cart dot txt is staged and scratch dot txt is a new file. Unstage, discard, then clean. The restore commands print nothing.

1.title: Undo local commits: amend and reset
1.text: Undo local commits: amend and reset. If the commit is not pushed, you may rewrite it. git commit the amend flag replaces the last commit: stage a forgotten file, then amend. git reset mode commit moves the branch back, and the mode decides what happens to the changes. the soft flag. Branch: Moved back. Staging area: Keeps the undone changes staged. Working tree: Unchanged. the mixed flag (default). Branch: Moved back. Staging area: Reset: changes unstaged. Working tree: Unchanged. the hard flag. Branch: Moved back. Staging area: Reset. Working tree: Reset: changes gone. Try it. The same commit, undone three ways. Each git reset the hard flag returns to the commit d eight a nine five e seven, and your hash will differ.

1.title: Undo local commits: amend and reset, continued
1.text: Undo local commits: amend and reset. The soft reset shows the file staged, the mixed reset shows it modified but unstaged, and the hard reset prints nothing because the tree is clean again. A hard reset also throws away uncommitted edits to tracked files, and it leaves untracked files alone. Tip: Use the soft flag or the mixed flag to keep your work, and the hard flag only when you mean to throw it away. Uncommitted changes are in no commit, so even the reflog cannot return them.

1.title: Undo shared commits: revert and cherry-pick
1.text: Undo shared commits: revert and cherry-pick. Once a commit is pushed, do not rewrite it. In the lab, Ada reset her branch and committed again: her push was rejected as a non-fast-forward. git revert hash instead adds a new commit that undoes the old one. History stays intact, so the push is normal and teammates pull it as a fast-forward. Try it. Revert the last commit.

1.title: Undo shared commits: revert and cherry-pick, continued
1.text: Undo shared commits: revert and cherry-pick. The message says "This reverts commit" and the hash. The original commit stays in the log. Reverting a merge. A merge commit has two parents, so Git cannot guess which side to keep. It stops with "is a merge but no -m option was given". Add dash m one: parent one is the branch you merged into, so the work that the merged branch brought is removed and the rest stays. The old history stays, too. Merging the same branch again now says "Already up to date" and brings nothing. To get the feature back, revert the revert.

1.title: Undo shared commits: revert and cherry-pick, continued
1.text: Undo shared commits: revert and cherry-pick. Cherry-pick. git cherry pick hash copies one commit from another branch onto the current one, with the same message and a new hash. dash x adds "(cherry picked from commit...)" to the message. If both sides changed the same lines, it conflicts like a merge, and git cherry pick the abort flag puts everything back. Tip: Pushed means revert, not rewrite. A revert is a normal new commit that everyone can pull.

1.title: Stash: park work without committing
1.text: Stash: park work without committing. Stash saves your uncommitted changes on a shelf and gives you a clean working tree. Use it when you must switch branches in the middle of something. git stash push dash m text. Saves tracked changes with a label. git stash push dash u. Also saves untracked files, which stay behind by default. git stash list. Lists entries, newest first: stash at zero. git stash pop. Re-applies the newest entry and removes it. git stash apply. Re-applies it and keeps the entry. git stash drop. Deletes the entry. git stash branch name. New branch from the commit the stash was made on, applies it, drops it.

1.title: Stash: park work without committing, continued
1.text: Stash: park work without committing. Try it. Park an edit, then bring it back. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.text: Stash: park work without committing. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Stash: park work without committing, continued
1.text: Stash: park work without committing. If the file changed on the branch in the meantime, pop stops with a conflict and keeps the entry, so nothing is lost. stash branch is the clean way out: the new branch starts where the stash began, so the changes apply without a conflict. Tip: Give every stash a label with dash m, and prefer pop over leaving a long list. Entries called "W I P on main" are impossible to tell apart a week later.

2.title: The safety net: the reflog
2.text: The safety net: the reflog. The reflog is a local diary of every place head and each branch pointed. A commit that no branch reaches is not deleted yet, and the reflog still names it. It exists only in your clone and is cleaned up after a while. Try it. Throw two commits away, then take them back.

2.title: The safety net: the reflog, continued
2.text: The safety net: the reflog. head at one means "where head was one move ago". If you did other things in between, read the list and use the hash. A deleted branch. git branch dash d refuses a branch with unmerged commits. git branch dash D deletes it and prints Deleted branch feature slash wishlist was c one three nine three zero zero. That hash is your way back: git branch feature slash wishlist c one three nine three zero zero.

2.title: The safety net: the reflog, continued
2.text: The safety net: the reflog. An edit, not staged. git restore file. A staged file. git restore the staged flag file. Last commit, wrong message or file, not pushed. git commit the amend flag. Commits not pushed, keep the work. git reset the soft flag or the mixed flag. Commits not pushed, throw them away. git reset the hard flag headabout N. A commit already pushed. git revert hash. A lost commit or branch. git reflog, then git branch or git reset the hard flag. Tip: When something vanishes, stop and run git reflog before anything else. The commit is almost always still there.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. git status dash s shows M cart dot txt and?? scratch dot txt. You want to unstage cart dot txt and keep your edit. Which command does that? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: git restore the staged flag cart dot txt, which unstages it. the staged flag removes the file from the staging area and leaves the edit in the working tree.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. You committed to main by mistake and have not pushed. You want the commit undone and its changes left staged. Which command fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: git reset the soft flag head tilde one, which leaves them staged. the soft flag moves the branch back and keeps the changes in the staging area.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A bad commit is on main, and teammates have already pulled it. What is the safest way to undo it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: git revert hash, then a normal git push. A revert is a new commit on top, so nobody's history is rewritten and the push is accepted.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. git revert head on a merge commit prints "is a merge but no -m option was given". What do you run next? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: git revert dash m one head, which keeps the first parent's side. Parent one is the branch that was merged into, so dash m one removes only what the merged branch brought.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. git branch dash D feature slash wishlist printed Deleted branch feature slash wishlist was c one three nine three zero zero. You need the branch back. What do you run? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Recreate it with git branch feature slash wishlist c one three nine three zero zero. The printed hash is the old tip, and git branch name hash creates a branch there again.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. You edited cart dot txt and created a new untracked file notes dot txt. You run git stash push dash m wip. What does git status show? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: cart dot txt is stashed, and notes dot txt is untracked. A stash takes tracked changes only, unless you add dash u.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Which command unstages a file but keeps the edit? Answer: git restore the staged flag file. Question two. Which option of git clean previews what would be removed? Answer: dash n, the dry run. Question three. Which command replaces the last unpushed commit with a corrected one? Answer: git commit the amend flag.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What does git revert do to history? Answer: It adds a new commit that undoes an older one and rewrites nothing. Question five. Which command copies one commit onto your current branch? Answer: git cherry pick hash. Question six. Which command lists where head has been, so you can find a lost commit? Answer: git reflog.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Discard and unstage: git restore file discards; git restore the staged flag file unstages. Clean: git clean dash n previews; dash f deletes untracked files; dash d directories; dash x ignored files. Amend: replaces the last commit; only before you push. Reset: the soft flag keeps changes staged; the mixed flag keeps them unstaged; the hard flag throws them away. Revert: new commit that undoes an old one; for pushed work. Cherry-pick: copies one commit with a new hash; dash x notes the source; the abort flag on conflict. Stash: push dash m, dash u, list, pop, apply, drop, branch. Reflog: local history of head.
